  "text": "The elevator in my building has a button for a basement that doesn't exist.

Management says it's a manufacturing error. Press it and nothing happens.

Last Thursday, I pressed it while carrying groceries.

The elevator went down.

Below the parking garage, the doors opened onto a corridor lined with apartment doors. Mine was nearest.

Same number. Same scratch beneath the lock.

From inside, I heard my mother washing dishes.

She's been dead for six years.

“Put the milk away,” she called. “Before it turns.”

I pressed the lobby button until the doors closed.

Upstairs, my groceries were still in their bags, except for the milk.

I found it in the refrigerator.

On Friday, I took the stairs. There were thirteen flights instead of twelve. On the extra landing, someone had left my childhood shoes, toes pointing toward a door.

I stepped over them.

That evening, my mother called.

Her number appeared as BASEMENT.

“You can't keep making me come upstairs,” she said.

I unplugged the phone. It was a landline I hadn't used in years.

Saturday morning, management sent a notice apologizing for noise during renovations. Residents were asked to ignore any unfamiliar floors.

I packed a suitcase.

The stairs ended at the basement corridor. So did the fire escape.

Behind my duplicate door, dishes clinked.

“Where are you going?” my mother asked.

I told her I wanted to go home.

The washing stopped.

Then she opened the door, wearing the coat I'd buried her in.

Over her shoulder, I saw my kitchen. My groceries sat on the counter.

She took the suitcase from me.

“Did you forget the milk?”"
}
